appraisal_events.evidence: « il y avait au moins deux Gilberte » ; la moins bonne, héritée de sa mère, est « libre de se réjouir de plaisirs peu nobles » et se trahit par « une réflexion mesquine, un ricanement fourbe » ; elle manque le rendez-vous qu’elle avait proposé et « se sentait en faute et désirait éviter les explications », tandis que le bon regard franc et le cœur aux « vues larges » viennent de son père.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator anatomizes Gilberte as a split creature and grants the father-derived half generosity only in order to expose the mother-derived half as petty, deceitful, and unreliable; the passage's main narrated point is that lesser Gilberte, which lowers her locally.

appraisal_events.evidence: Swann signale « avec quelle intelligence, quelle justesse imprévue l’actrice disait à Œnone : "Tu le savais !" » et le narrateur concède « Il avait raison » ; mais « toute artiste intelligente eût pu l’acquérir », et « peut-on employer ce mot de "trouver" quand il s’agit de trouver quelque chose qui ne serait pas différent si on l’avait reçu ».
appraisal_events.explanation: Swann's admiring remark is conceded as correct and then dismantled: the intonation's very intelligibility makes it transferable and so not essentially hers, so the closing movement withholds the admiration it seems to grant.

status_effects.explanation: The sustained portrait grants her a good, paternal half but concludes on pettiness, sly mockery, broken appointments, and bad faith, so her local standing clearly falls.

The inherited defects are explicitly assigned to Odette — the mesquine heart, the evasive look recalled from the days when she lied to Swann about her lovers — so she is discredited through the same analysis.

The comparative structure gives Swann the good half of his daughter — the frank gaze, the generous heart — and the scene stages her clinging affection and his tender answer, raising him locally against Odette.
Her praised intonation is redescribed as an idea any intelligent actress could reproduce, denying her the credit of having genuinely found it.

ambiguities: Swann's local elevation is real but qualified: the same paragraph frames him as a man whose generosity to women earned no gratitude and who has become an « mari incurieux et prudent » resigned to evasive answers, so the positive movement carries pathos rather than straightforward credit.

The closing movement can be read as directed less at la Berma herself — her delivery is explicitly granted intelligence and justesse, and Swann's judgment is endorsed as right — than at the narrator's inability to found admiration on demonstrable reasons; the negative charge falls on the transferability of the effect rather than on the actress's performance.
